title: Bought the Newport Ben Franklin franchise with borrowed family capital
statement: Months after leaving the Army, Walton combined a twenty-thousand-dollar loan from his father-in-law Leland Robson with five thousand dollars of Army savings to buy a Butler Brothers Ben Franklin variety store in Newport, Arkansas, at age twenty-six, committing to the franchise system's small-town merchandising while undercutting rival stores on price by finding lower-cost suppliers.
outcome: Sales climbed from eighty thousand dollars to two hundred twenty-five thousand dollars within three years, tripling the store's volume. The success attracted the store's landlord, P. K. Holmes, who wanted the location and franchise rights for his son and refused to renew the lease because Walton had never secured a renewal option.

title: Rebuilt from the Newport eviction with the Bentonville 5&10
statement: After losing the Newport lease, Walton sold the store's inventory and fixtures to Holmes for fifty thousand dollars and negotiated a purchase on Bentonville's downtown square conditioned on a ninety-nine-year lease to expand into the shop next door. When the neighboring owner refused six times, Walton's father-in-law quietly paid twenty thousand dollars to secure the lease, and the new store opened with a one-day remodeling sale on May 9, 1950.
outcome: The store Walton bought had been doing seventy-two thousand dollars in annual sales; it reached one hundred five thousand dollars in the first year, one hundred forty thousand in the second, and one hundred seventy-five thousand in the third. The location now serves as the Walmart Museum on the Bentonville square.

title: Opened the first Wal-Mart Discount City in Rogers, Arkansas
statement: Walton placed his first discount store in Rogers, Arkansas, a small town the major discount chains ignored, combining a format studied at Ann & Hope with a name borrowed from Sol Price's FedMart, staffing it on his small-town price philosophy, and committing the store to marketing American-made products sourced from domestic manufacturers who could meet foreign pricing.
outcome: Within five years the company reached eighteen Arkansas stores and nine million dollars in sales, crossing into Missouri and Oklahoma in 1968. By 1990 Walmart had become the largest American retailer by revenue, and the original Rogers site remains a landmark of the company's origin story.

title: Took Walmart public while keeping the family's control
statement: After incorporating in Delaware in October 1969 and renaming the company Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., Walton began public trading on October 1, 1970, the same year the company opened its Bentonville home office and first distribution center while operating thirty-eight stores with forty-four-point-two million dollars in sales, using the proceeds to finance steady expansion while the family retained its controlling stake.
outcome: A New York Stock Exchange listing followed, and the first stock split came at forty-seven dollars a share. The Walton family still controls the company through the Walton Enterprises holding company, which held forty-three percent of the stock as of 2017 alongside a family trust's additional five percent.

title: Launched Sam's Club against Sol Price's warehouse format
statement: After dining with Price Club founder Sol Price, from whom he admitted borrowing as many ideas as from anyone in retailing, Walton opened the first Sam's Wholesale Club in Midwest City, Oklahoma, on April 7, 1983, adopting the membership warehouse club model of bulk merchandise, pallet merchandising, and no-frills stores carrying his own first name.
outcome: Renamed Sam's Club in 1990 and expanded through the 1987 SuperSaver acquisition of twenty-four clubs and the 1993 purchase of PACE clubs from Kmart, the division became the second-largest American warehouse club with ninety billion dollars in sales by fiscal 2025, behind only Costco.

title: Handed vendors the data with Retail Link
statement: David Glass and Rob Walton managed the development of Retail Link beginning in 1985, Walmart's proprietary trend-forecasting software that gave suppliers direct access to store-level sales data and enabled vendor-managed inventory arrangements in which vendors themselves timed replenishment using electronic data interchange and statistical forecasting.
outcome: Retail Link became the connective tissue of Walmart's supply chain — the commercial interface of the satellite network completed in 1987 — and a model widely copied across the retail industry, cementing the supplier collaboration practices used by Walmart and Procter & Gamble.

title: Built the largest private satellite network in America
statement: Walton completed a twenty-four-million-dollar private satellite network in 1987 linking every store to the Bentonville home office with two-way voice and data transmission and one-way video communications, allowing the corporate office to track inventory and sales and to communicate instantly with stores.
outcome: Paired with barcode readers in ninety percent of stores by 1988, the network underpinned the contiguous hub-and-spoke distribution expansion credited with Walmart's outperformance between 1980 and 2000, when the company reached 1,198 stores and fifteen-point-nine billion dollars in sales by its twenty-fifth anniversary.

title: Passed the chairmanship to Rob Walton after ceding the CEO seat to David Glass
statement: Walton stepped down as chief executive in February 1988 in favor of David Glass while remaining chairman of the board, and after his death on April 5, 1992, the board named his eldest son, S. Robson Walton, chairman on April 7, keeping family control alongside professional management through the transition.
outcome: Rob Walton held the chairmanship until 2015, Glass served as chief executive until January 2000 while the store count grew from 123 in 1976 to more than 4,000 by 2005, and the Walton family still owns roughly half of Walmart through Walton Enterprises, making it the largest family-controlled public company in the world.
